demo.space.description: Dr. Watson's notebook, 1881–1894, in a separate space. Removed with one button; your own records are untouched.
demo.notice: This is Dr. Watson's notebook — a demo. Your own records are under “My data”.
demo.deleteConfirm: Delete the demo along with everything you added to it? Your records under “My data” will not be affected.
demo.menu.title: Getting started
demo.scope.people.note: Those with whom these years were spent. Holmes first; the others around him.
demo.scope.holmes.note: Chemistry — profound; literature — nil. The violin; tobacco in a Persian slipper.
demo.scope.lestrade.note: Scotland Yard. Comes round when he cannot manage on his own.
demo.scope.moriarty.note: A mathematician. “The Napoleon of crime” — Holmes's words.
demo.scope.hudson.note: Landlady of 221B. Puts up with pistol practice on the wall and the chemistry.
demo.scope.mycroft.note: The elder brother. The Diogenes Club.
demo.scope.places.note: The rooms, houses and moors where it all happened. Of them all I truly know only 221B.
demo.scope.hall.note: Dartmoor. The yew alley, the gate onto the moor.
demo.scope.mire.note: The bog. Only Stapleton knows the path.
demo.scope.cases.note: The ones I wrote up. Dozens I did not.
demo.scope.scarlet.note: March 1881. Lauriston Gardens, RACHE on the wall, a cabman in our sitting room. The first case I saw from the beginning.
demo.scope.band.note: April 1883. One night at Stoke Moran: the bell-rope, the ventilator, a whistle at three.
demo.scope.hound.note: October 1889. Dartmoor: an inheritance, a legend and a hound with a phosphorescent muzzle. Three weeks — as I thought — without Holmes.
demo.scope.final.note: April–May 1891. Professor Moriarty, the flight across the Continent and the falls above Meiringen. The case I believed for three years to be the last.
demo.scope.practice.note: Medicine. What I live on between cases.
demo.period.1880s.note: Ten years with Holmes: from the laboratory at Barts to the islet in the Grimpen Mire. I wrote up the cases that can be told — Lauriston Gardens, Stoke Moran, Baskerville Hall — and kept silent about dozens of others. In those years I married, bought a practice, and learned to tell observing from seeing — not entirely.
demo.period.1881.note: The year we met. I came back from Afghanistan with a shattered shoulder and no plans; Stamford brought me to a man who knew me for an army surgeon within a second. I do not remember the day — and, judging by the arguments of the experts, I do not remember it correctly. The first case — Lauriston Gardens: RACHE on the wall, a cabman in handcuffs in our sitting room.
demo.period.1883-04.note: One night at Stoke Moran: a girl in black at daybreak, a bent poker, a bell-rope that leads nowhere, and a whistle at three in the morning. The quickest case in this notebook — and the most frightening.
demo.period.1889-10.note: Dartmoor. Three weeks that I spent, as I thought, without Holmes: the yew alley, a candle in the window, a convict on the moor, a man on the tor. Read it by the reports: the 13th, the 15th, the diary of the 16th and 17th — and my theory of the 10th, of which I am ashamed to this day.
demo.period.1891.note: The year I buried my friend. After Dartmoor we hardly saw each other — marriage and the practice had drawn me into another life — which made it the more terrible to find him in my consulting room with his knuckles torn. Professor Moriarty, the flight across the Continent, the falls above Meiringen and three pages under the cigarette case. The entries after May are practice only.
demo.period.1894.note: He came back. Everything I wrote in 1891 was true — except the main thing. The murder in Park Lane, an old man with books in my consulting room, a wax bust in the window, and Colonel Moran in the empty house opposite.
demo.trace.start.desc:
This is my notebook of the years with Sherlock Holmes — from the winter of 1881, when chance threw me, a retired army surgeon with neither money nor kin, in his way, to the spring of 1894, when he came back from the dead. I wrote while the trail was fresh, the way a doctor writes up a case history: facts, not conclusions — that is what Holmes demanded. Every entry knows what it belongs to — a person, a place or a case — so follow the links. “To the selected” takes you to the entry's time. The periods on the left are chapters, with my notes on how each one ended.
→ next: “You have been in Afghanistan, I perceive”
demo.trace.afghan.desc: The second Afghan campaign ended for me at Maiwand: a Jezail bullet shattered the bone and grazed the artery; then enteric fever at Peshawar; then the troopship Orontes to Portsmouth. The Government allowed me eleven shillings and sixpence a day for nine months of mending. Neither kith nor kin in England; I put up at a hotel in the Strand and spent more than I should have. London, that great cesspool into which all the loungers of the Empire are drained — and I was one of them.
demo.trace.stamford.desc: Stamford had been a dresser under me at Barts. We ran into each other at the Criterion bar and lunched at the Holborn. I complained that I could not find rooms within my means, and he said that only that morning he had heard the same complaint from a fellow at the chemical laboratory: he had found good rooms but could not afford them alone. “He is a little queer in his ideas. You mustn't blame me if you don't get on with him.” We went round to the laboratory.
demo.trace.meet: “You have been in Afghanistan, I perceive”
demo.trace.meet.desc:
He was standing at the bench with a test-tube, crying out that he had found a reagent precipitated by haemoglobin and by nothing else — blood stains could now be told from rust. Then he held out his hand and said: “You have been in Afghanistan, I perceive.” I could not think how he knew it, and he explained only some days later: the tan, the military bearing, the injured arm. That is how I came to know Sherlock Holmes. I do not remember the day — and, judging by the arguments of those who have tried to reconstruct the chronology, I do not remember it correctly.
→ next: 221B
demo.trace.rooms: Took the rooms at 221B Baker Street
demo.trace.rooms.desc: We looked over the rooms the next day and took them on the spot: two bedrooms, a large sitting room with two broad windows onto the street, and a landlady, Mrs. Hudson. Holmes moved in that evening, I the next morning. He plays the violin — sometimes music, sometimes merely drawing the bow across the strings — conducts experiments, and can lie on the sofa for days without a word. Visitors come to him: a police inspector, a young girl, a rag-and-bone man. What he did for a living I did not then know.
demo.trace.list: A list of what Holmes knows
demo.trace.list.desc: A few days on, I drew up a list of what my fellow-lodger knew and what he did not. Literature — nil. Philosophy — nil. Astronomy — nil: he did not know that the earth goes round the sun, and said he would do his best to forget it. Botany — variable: belladonna, opium and poisons generally — profound; practical gardening — nothing. Chemistry — profound. Anatomy — accurate but unsystematic. Sensational literature — immense. Plays the violin well, a boxer and a swordsman, has a good practical knowledge of British law. I read the list through and threw it into the fire: there was no sense to be made of it. The answer came of its own accord: Holmes is the world's only “consulting detective”; people come to him when they have failed.
demo.trace.gregson: A letter from Gregson of Scotland Yard
demo.trace.gregson.desc: A letter came in the morning from Tobias Gregson: in an empty house at 3 Lauriston Gardens an American, Enoch Drebber, has been found dead — no wound, but blood; would Holmes help. Holmes on Gregson: “The smartest of the Scotland Yarders; he and Lestrade are the pick of a bad lot.” He did not want to go — “they will get all the credit” — but he went, and took me with him. The first case I saw from the very beginning.
demo.trace.scarlet.intent: Work out who wrote RACHE on the wall
demo.trace.scarlet.intent.desc: In the bare room, a body; on the wall, at eye level, RACHE written in blood. Lestrade was triumphant: the murderer had meant to write “Rachel” and been interrupted. Holmes went over the floor and the walls with a tape measure and a lens, and said the murderer was a man six feet tall, smoked Trichinopoly cigars and had come in a cab — and that RACHE is German for “revenge”, written to put the police off the scent. There was also a woman's wedding ring. I had yet to decide whether he was a charlatan or a genius.
demo.trace.scarlet.case: Three days from Gregson's letter to the arrest. There was no fee — in those days Holmes worked for the problem's sake.
demo.trace.hope: The cabman Jefferson Hope taken in our sitting room
demo.trace.hope.desc:
Holmes advertised the found ring in the papers, then had a street urchin fetch a cab. The cabman came into the sitting room, bent to help with the trunk — and Holmes snapped the handcuffs on him. Jefferson Hope, an American, had hunted for twenty years the two men who destroyed his betrothed, Lucy Ferrier, in Utah, and had run both of them down in London; the cab was his way of getting close. He died of an aneurism in his cell before he could be tried, and I wrote his story down whole. The credit, as Holmes had foretold, went to Gregson and Lestrade.
→ next: April 1883
demo.trace.stoner: Helen Stoner, a quarter past seven in the morning
demo.trace.stoner.desc: Holmes woke me at a quarter past seven: a client was waiting in the sitting room. Helen Stoner, thirty, all in black, shivering — and not from cold. She lives at Stoke Moran in Surrey with her stepfather, Dr. Grimesby Roylott, a man of ungovernable temper who came back from India, where he had served a term for killing a servant, and keeps gypsies, a cheetah and a baboon about the grounds. Two years ago her sister Julia died a fortnight before her wedding, crying out about “the speckled band”; on the nights before her death she had heard a low whistle. Now Helen is engaged, repairs have moved her into Julia's room — and last night she heard the whistle.
demo.trace.band.intent: Work out what killed Julia Stoner — before it comes for Helen
demo.trace.band.intent.desc: Holmes took it up at once. What killed Julia in a locked room without a mark of violence — and what now waits for Helen. We have until nightfall.
demo.trace.roylott: Dr. Roylott burst in and bent the poker
demo.trace.roylott.desc: An hour after Helen left, the door flew open: a huge man in a top hat, a face seamed with wrinkles, yellow eyes. Dr. Roylott had tracked his stepdaughter. “Holmes the meddler. Holmes the busybody. Holmes the Scotland Yard jack-in-office.” He seized the poker, bent it into a curve and left. Holmes picked the poker up and straightened it with one effort: “Had he been a shade less rude, I might have shown him that my grip is not much more feeble than his own.”
demo.trace.stoke.desc: In the afternoon, while Roylott was in London, we went down to Stoke Moran. Helen showed us the rooms. By her bed hangs a bell-rope that leads nowhere: “pull it — nothing”. The ventilator in the wall opens not to the air but into her stepfather's room. The bed is clamped to the floor — it cannot be moved away from the rope. In Roylott's room: an iron safe, a saucer of milk, and a dog-lash tied into a loop. Holmes grew darker with every find: “When a doctor does go wrong, he is the first of criminals.”
demo.trace.vigil.desc: We took a room at the Crown Inn opposite the manor and waited for the signal — a lamp in Helen's window. We climbed the wall and got into her room; Holmes with his cane and matches, I with my revolver. “Do not go asleep; your very life may depend upon it.” We sat in utter darkness, hearing the church clock strike — twelve, one, two, three.
demo.trace.whistle: Three in the morning. A whistle. Holmes lashes at the rope with his cane
demo.trace.whistle.desc:
At three o'clock a light showed through the ventilator and there came a soft hissing. Holmes sprang up, struck a match and lashed furiously at the bell-rope with his cane; I could see nothing. Then a whistle — and then a dreadful cry from the next room. Roylott sat dead in his chair, round his head “the speckled band”: a swamp adder, the deadliest snake in India. He had sent it down the rope through the ventilator and whistled it back; Holmes's blows drove it home to its master. “I am indirectly responsible for his death, and it will not weigh very heavily upon my conscience.”
→ next: October 1889
demo.trace.band.case: Two days. No fee was taken: Helen had nothing, and Roylott held the purse strings of the inheritance.
demo.trace.mycroft.meet.desc: For seven years I had taken Holmes for a man without relations: he never spoke of anyone. One summer evening, talking of heredity, he suddenly said that he has a brother, Mycroft, seven years his senior, with keener powers of observation than his own, but indolent, and never one to test a conclusion on his feet. Mycroft audits the books in some of the government departments and lives between his rooms in Pall Mall, his office and the Diogenes Club, where talking is forbidden. We went there. A huge, corpulent man with sharp grey eyes. The brothers stood at the window and read a passer-by between them: an old soldier, a sergeant, lately widowed, two children. I understood that Holmes is not the only one.
demo.trace.charles: The death of Sir Charles Baskerville in the yew alley
demo.trace.charles.desc: This I learned later, from Dr. Mortimer. Sir Charles Baskerville, a widower who had made his fortune in South Africa and come home to restore the family Hall on Dartmoor, went out in the evening, as he always did, to smoke in the yew alley. In the morning Barrymore the butler found him dead by the gate onto the moor, his face distorted, no mark of violence. The inquest said: his heart. Mortimer, Sir Charles's friend and physician, told us what he had not told the inquest: a little way from the body he had seen the footprints of a gigantic hound.
demo.trace.mortimer: Dr. Mortimer left his stick behind
demo.trace.mortimer.desc: Last evening, while we were out, a visitor called and left his stick behind — a thick piece of wood with a silver band: “To James Mortimer, M.R.C.S., from his friends of the C.C.H., 1884”. Holmes, from the stick: a country doctor, walks a great deal, absent-minded, owns a dog “larger than a terrier and smaller than a mastiff”. This morning Mortimer came back — with a curly-haired spaniel. He is a doctor on Dartmoor and was Sir Charles Baskerville's friend and executor. He has brought an old manuscript and a newspaper and wants advice: the heir arrives from Canada tomorrow, and Mortimer fears for him.
demo.trace.legend.desc: Mortimer read aloud the manuscript of 1742 that Sir Charles had kept: Hugo Baskerville, a profane and godless rake, carried off a yeoman's daughter; she fled across the moor; he swore away his soul and set the hounds on her; his companions found both dead, and over Hugo's body stood “a great, black beast, shaped like a hound, yet larger than any hound”. Holmes yawned: “Interesting to a collector of fairy tales.” Then Mortimer read the notice of Sir Charles's death — and told us about the footprints.
demo.trace.hound.intent: Work out what killed Sir Charles — before it gets to Sir Henry
demo.trace.hound.intent.desc:
Holmes has taken the case. We do not know what killed Sir Charles — the hound of the legend, a man, or fear — but we know that the heir, Sir Henry, arrives tomorrow, and that whoever waited on the moor is waiting for him too. Mortimer brings him to us in the morning. Everything is to be written down, even what seems a trifle: facts, not guesses.
→ the steps are below; read them by date
demo.trace.henry.desc: Henry Baskerville, Sir Charles's nephew and the last of the line, a farmer from Canada, thirty years old, sturdy, dark-eyed. He came with Mortimer straight from his hotel and brought a letter he had received that morning — words cut out of a newspaper. Holmes told him everything; Sir Henry heard him out and answered that there is no devil in hell and no man upon earth who can prevent him from going to the home of his own people. Holmes said that in that case I would go with him.
demo.trace.step.boot: Work out why Sir Henry's boot was stolen
demo.trace.step.boot.desc: A trifle that would not let Holmes rest: at the hotel one of Sir Henry's boots went missing. What does anyone want with one boot?
demo.trace.step.barrymore.desc: A bearded man in the cab — and Barrymore the butler, Mortimer says, wears a black beard. He was the only one at the Hall the night Sir Charles died, and the will left him five hundred pounds. Holmes's telegram proved nothing — it was handed to the wife. To be checked on Dartmoor.
demo.trace.step.convict.desc: Selden, the Notting Hill murderer, escaped from Princetown prison, is hiding on the moor. If a beast walks the moor, somebody feeds it and somebody directs it. To be checked.
demo.trace.step.tor: Find out who the man on the tor is
demo.trace.step.tor.desc: At night a tall man stood on the tor in the moonlight — not Selden — and melted away. Find out who he is.
demo.trace.step.stapleton.desc: Stapleton of Merripit House knew who I was before I had introduced myself; he knows everything about the legend and about Sir Henry; he lives at the very edge of the mire and alone knows the path across it. And his sister, taking me for Sir Henry, whispered that I must go back to London. Who is he?
demo.trace.step.night.desc: Holmes's plan: Sir Henry dines at Stapleton's and walks home across the moor alone — as on the night Sir Charles died. Holmes, Lestrade and I wait by the path with revolvers. Sir Henry has been told only “go home by the straight path”.
demo.trace.letter: A letter to Sir Henry made of cut-out words
demo.trace.letter.desc: The letter reached Sir Henry at the Northumberland Hotel in the morning, though nobody was supposed to know he had come: “As you value your life or your reason keep away from the moor.” Every word cut from a newspaper and pasted on, except “moor” — that one written in by hand. Holmes held the sheet up to his eyes: the type of yesterday's Times leader, an article on free trade; cut with nail scissors; the writer feared his hand would be known.
demo.trace.boots: Sir Henry's new brown boot has gone missing
demo.trace.boots.desc: At the hotel Sir Henry lost a new brown boot, bought the day before in the Strand — one of the pair. Sir Henry made a fuss. The next day the boot turned up, but an old black one, well worn, had gone. Holmes pricked up his ears as though this mattered more than the letter. I could not see why.
demo.trace.cab: A bearded man followed Sir Henry from cab No. 2704
demo.trace.cab.desc: We followed Sir Henry and Mortimer on foot down Regent Street and saw a cab crawling after them; a man with a black beard looked out of its window. He noticed us and shouted to the cabman to drive on. Holmes took the number — 2704. In the evening the cabman, John Clayton, came to Baker Street: his fare had said he was a detective and given his name as Mr. Sherlock Holmes. Holmes burst out laughing: “We have been checkmated in London.”
demo.trace.wire.1: Holmes wired Barrymore at Baskerville Hall, marked “to be delivered into his own hand”: if he is on Dartmoor, he cannot have been sitting in a cab in Regent Street. The postmaster replied that the telegram had been delivered — to Barrymore's wife; he himself was up in the loft. The answer proved nothing.
demo.trace.paddington.desc: Saturday, the 10:30 from Paddington. Holmes saw us off on the platform: he stays behind — “a case of blackmail keeps me in London” — and I am to write about everything and never let Sir Henry go out on the moor alone. Three of us travel: Sir Henry, Mortimer and I. Mortimer's spaniel is in the luggage van.
demo.trace.hall.arrive.desc: We drove across the moor in an open wagonette. By the road stood a soldier with a rifle: Selden, the murderer, has broken out of Princetown. The Hall is a dark house with two towers, the portraits of the Baskervilles on the walls of the great hall. Barrymore the butler — tall, black-bearded — and his wife. In the night I lay awake and heard a woman sobbing in the house.
demo.trace.stapleton.meet.desc: On the moor a man with a butterfly net caught me up: Jack Stapleton of Merripit House, a naturalist, once a schoolmaster in the north. He knew who I was — from Mortimer. He showed me the Grimpen Mire: before my eyes a moor pony went down into it, and Stapleton said he knows the only path. Then a long, low moan rolled over the moor; the country folk say it is the Hound of the Baskervilles. Afterwards his sister Beryl came up — a beauty — took me for Sir Henry, and whispered that I must go back to London.
demo.trace.hyp.barrymore: My theory: Barrymore is the murderer
demo.trace.hyp.barrymore.desc: My theory, and I write it down so that I can test it later: the murderer is Barrymore. He lied about the telegram; he was the only one in the house when Sir Charles died; he came into money under the will; on our very first night in the house his wife was weeping, and he said that nobody had wept. And now, for the second night running, I have seen him at the window in the west wing: he holds a candle to the glass and stares out over the moor. The beard is the same as the man's in the cab.
demo.trace.report1.desc:
First report to Holmes, Baskerville Hall, 13 October. The main thing is Barrymore: two nights running he has stood with a candle at the window of the west wing, looking out over the moor; Sir Henry saw the same. By day Barrymore said he had been seeing that the windows were fastened. Also: Stapleton, his sister and her strange warning; the howl on the moor; the pony in the mire.
→ next: “A light on the moor”
demo.trace.light: A light on the moor answers Barrymore's candle
demo.trace.light.desc: Sir Henry and I lay in wait for Barrymore at the window. He said nothing; his wife did: Selden, the escaped convict, is her younger brother; they carry food out to him; the candle is a signal, and a light on the moor answers it. We went out onto the moor to take Selden, saw his face in the candlelight — a beast's — and lost him. Barrymore is in the clear, and I am ashamed of my theory.
demo.trace.report2.desc:
Second report, 15 October. Barrymore told us one thing more: on the night he died Sir Charles was waiting at the gate for a woman — a scrap of a letter survives, signed “L. L.”, asking him to burn it. Mortimer knows a Laura Lyons of Coombe Tracey, old Frankland's daughter, deserted by her husband. And the main thing: while we chased Selden, a tall, thin man stood on the tor in the moonlight, motionless, like the spirit of that place. Not Selden.
→ next: “The stone hut”
demo.trace.diary16.desc: From my diary. Fog all day; somewhere on the moor a hound is howling, and it is not the wind. Sir Henry goes pale and says nothing. He calls at the Stapletons' more often than he should: Beryl.
demo.trace.hut: The stone hut on the moor
demo.trace.hut.desc:
Old Frankland, the litigant, showed me through his telescope a boy carrying a bundle onto the moor — “to the convict”. I followed the boy's trail and found, in a Bronze Age stone hut, fresh ashes, a blanket and a note: “Dr. Watson has gone to Coombe Tracey.” I sat down with my revolver to wait for the tenant. He came in with the words: “It is a lovely evening, my dear Watson.” Holmes had been living on the moor all this time; the boy Cartwright brought him food, and my reports came here from Baker Street a day late. He told me the main thing: Beryl is not Stapleton's sister but his wife.
→ next: “A cry on the moor”
demo.trace.selden: A cry on the moor. The body in Sir Henry's clothes is Selden
demo.trace.selden.desc: We were walking towards the Hall when a cry rang out over the moor, then another, then a low rumble and silence. On the rocks lay a man in Sir Henry's tweed suit, his skull crushed. We took him for Sir Henry — but it was Selden: Barrymore had given him his master's old clothes. The hound had followed the scent of the boot stolen at the hotel. Stapleton appeared out of the dark with a cigar and asked whether it was Sir Henry. Holmes told him he returns to London tomorrow. The convict is dead, but the theory about him was wrong from the first.
demo.trace.portrait.desc: Dinner at the Hall. Holmes could not take his eyes off the portrait of Hugo Baskerville — the Hugo, of 1647. When Sir Henry had gone he raised a candle, covered the hat and the ringlets on the portrait with his hand — and Stapleton looked out at me. “An interesting instance of a throwback.” Stapleton is a Baskerville, the son of Sir Charles's younger brother Rodger, who fled to America. Should Sir Henry die — he inherits.
demo.trace.lyons.desc: In the morning we drove to Coombe Tracey to see Laura Lyons. She confessed: the letter to Sir Charles asking him to meet her at the gate at ten in the evening was hers — Stapleton dictated it, promised to marry her and to help with her divorce. But she never went to the meeting: Stapleton talked her out of it. When Holmes told her that Stapleton is married and that his “sister” is his wife, she told us everything.
demo.trace.wire.2: Holmes has sent to London for Lestrade: “Come with a warrant, the 5:40 train.” Lestrade is “the best of the professionals”, and Holmes wants his hands and his authority.
demo.trace.boot.answer: The boot was needed to give the hound the scent
demo.trace.boot.answer.desc: Now the boot makes sense too. Stapleton needed Sir Henry's scent to set the hound on him. The new boot did not yet smell of its owner — it was returned, and a worn one taken. A trifle, from which Holmes deduced that the beast was real.
demo.trace.hound.answer.desc: In the morning, walking back from the moor, Holmes put it all together, and I write it down so as not to lose a link. Stapleton is the son of Rodger Baskerville, Sir Charles's younger brother, who fled to America; under another name he kept a school in the north, went bankrupt and settled in Dartmoor, next to the inheritance. He bought the hound in London, from a dealer on the Fulham Road — the largest and most savage he could find — and kept it on an island in the mire, reached by a single path; with a phosphorus paste he made of it the ghost of the legend. Knowing Sir Charles had a weak heart, he used Laura Lyons to lure the old man to the gate on the moor and loosed the hound: it never touched him — he died of fright, and the footprints stayed on the soft ground a little way off. For Sir Henry he was preparing the same: the boot from the hotel to give the hound the scent, the "sister" Beryl — his wife, whom he beat to keep her silent. Had Sir Henry died, Stapleton would have come forward as the heir. That is what killed Sir Charles: not a legend, but a man with a plan. → next: “I reread my theory about Barrymore”
demo.trace.night.desc:
The night at Merripit House. We lay among the rocks by the path; fog crept in from the mire. At ten Sir Henry left the Stapletons' and set off across the moor. Out of the fog came the hound — enormous, black, its muzzle and eyes burning with fire. Holmes and I fired; it howled and tore on; we caught it up over Sir Henry, who lay on the ground — five shots, and it died. Phosphorus on the muzzle and the coat. Sir Henry lives. In the house we found Beryl, lashed to a post and covered in bruises: Stapleton had fled into the mire along the wands. In the morning we follow them.
→ next: 1891
demo.trace.revisit.barrymore.desc: Reread my theory about Barrymore, and I am ashamed. Everything I wrote down was true — and all of it led the wrong way. Holmes, when I told him so: “You saw, Watson, but you did not observe.”
demo.trace.hound.case: Twenty-four days — from the stick in our sitting room to the islet in the mire. Mortimer is taking Sir Henry round the world to mend his nerves. The fee is a nominal entry: Holmes never named me a sum.
demo.trace.mire.search.desc: Holmes and Lestrade followed the wands out to the islet. Sir Henry's old boot — there; Stapleton — not. The mire gives nothing back.
demo.trace.married.desc: After Dartmoor my life went its own way: I married and bought a practice in Paddington — surgery in the morning, calls until night. I see Holmes seldom: he neither likes visitors nor pays visits, and I learn of his cases from the papers before I hear of them from him. A few times I slept at Baker Street for the sake of an old case; otherwise I am a family doctor, one of thousands. There are few entries because there was little to enter.
demo.trace.moriarty.who.desc: In the evening Holmes told me what I had not known. Professor James Moriarty: a mathematician; at twenty-one he wrote a treatise on the binomial theorem, won a chair at a provincial university — and went into the shadows when rumours began to go about. Now he lives in London as an army coach. For years Holmes had felt one hand behind half of the crime in the city — “the Napoleon of crime, a spider in the centre of its web”. For three months he has been weaving his net; in three days, on Monday, the police will take the whole gang. Moriarty knows it.
demo.trace.moriarty: Holmes in my consulting room with skinned knuckles
demo.trace.moriarty.desc: Holmes came into my consulting room pale, with skinned knuckles, asked leave to close the shutters, and asked whether I had ever heard of Professor Moriarty. That morning the man himself had called at Baker Street — tall, thin, a domed forehead, his head swaying like a snake's — and said: “You have less frontal development than I should have expected.” He offered Holmes a way out; Holmes refused. During the day a van nearly ran Holmes down, a brick fell from a roof, and in Vere Street a man with a bludgeon went for him — hence the knuckles. Holmes asked me to go to the Continent with him until the net closes.
demo.trace.flight.desc: Following Holmes's instructions I sent my luggage to Victoria unaddressed, took a cab to the Lowther Arcade, ran straight through it, and at the far end a brougham was waiting; the cloaked driver was — I learned later — Mycroft. On the train Holmes sat in the compartment in the guise of an old Italian priest. On the platform, as the train drew out, stood Moriarty. We got off at Canterbury, let his special train go by, reached Brussels by way of Newhaven and Dieppe, then Strasbourg. There a telegram: the gang taken, Moriarty escaped. Geneva, the valley of the Rhône, the Gemmi Pass, Meiringen.
demo.trace.final.desc:
From Meiringen we walked out to the Reichenbach Falls. A boy caught us up with a note from the hotel: an Englishwoman dying of consumption asked for an English doctor. I went; Holmes stayed by the edge. At the hotel the landlord knew nothing — he had not written the note. I ran back for two hours. Holmes's alpenstock lay on the path; in the wet earth, two lines of footprints to the brink of the fall, none coming back. Under his cigarette case, three pages in his hand: he had known Moriarty was waiting for him, asked me to see to his papers, and said he could not wish a better end to his career. They fell together. I write it down as fact, because I cannot do otherwise.
→ next: 1894
demo.trace.practice.91.desc: Bought a practice in Kensington. Surgery from nine, calls until late at night; I work a great deal, because it is easier that way. I keep away from Baker Street.
demo.trace.published.desc: For two years I said nothing. Colonel James Moriarty published letters in defence of his brother's memory, and I was obliged to tell how it really was. I sent “The Final Problem” to the press — the only story I have written with a heavy heart.
demo.trace.hiatus.tibet: Two years in Tibet as the Norwegian Sigerson
demo.trace.hiatus.tibet.desc: On the evening of his return, by the fire at Baker Street, Holmes told me where he had been for three years. From Switzerland he went into Italy and then east: for two years he travelled through Tibet under the name of a Norwegian, Sigerson, reached Lhasa and spent some days with the head Lama. The papers wrote of the “remarkable explorations of a Norwegian named Sigerson” — I read them without knowing whom they meant. He could not let me know: three of Moriarty's gang were still at large, and one of them had watched him climb out from under the falls.
demo.trace.hiatus.persia.desc: From Tibet, through Persia; he entered Mecca as a pilgrim, then looked in on the Khalifa at Khartoum and reported what he saw to the Foreign Office. When exactly all this happened Holmes did not say, and I did not ask: he told it as if it were another man's life.
demo.trace.hiatus.montpellier: Montpellier: research into the coal-tar derivatives
demo.trace.hiatus.montpellier.desc: The last months before his return — Montpellier, in the south of France: a laboratory, research into the coal-tar derivatives, quiet. It was there that a London paper with the Park Lane murder found him. He understood that the man he had waited three years for had stepped out of the shadow, and he came back.
demo.trace.mycroft.desc: The only one who knew Holmes was alive was Mycroft. For three years he paid for the rooms in Baker Street, kept the papers and the experiments exactly as Holmes had left them, and sent money. To me he never said a word, though we met. Holmes: “I could not take the risk, Watson — you could not have held your tongue the way it had to be held.”
demo.trace.adair: The murder of Ronald Adair in Park Lane
demo.trace.adair.desc: All London is talking of the murder of Ronald Adair, second son of the Earl of Maynooth: on 30 March he was shot in his own sitting room at 427 Park Lane, through the open window — and beneath the window a flower bed without a single footprint, and no man could have climbed up or down. The door was locked from the inside. On the table, money and a sheet of paper with a tally of card winnings. A soft-nosed revolver bullet, expanding. Since Holmes has been gone I follow the criminal news and try his methods against it; this case I could not make them fit.
demo.trace.moran.intent: Take the man who shot Adair
demo.trace.moran.intent.desc: From the first evening Holmes knew whom to look for: the man who shot Adair, and the man who saw him alive at the falls. They are one and the same, and tonight he will come for Holmes. Take him — and close the last of what Moriarty left behind.
demo.trace.bookseller: The old bookseller I bumped into near Park Lane came to apologise
demo.trace.bookseller.desc: In the afternoon I went to Park Lane to look at Adair's house, and in the crowd of idlers I knocked into a bent old man with an armful of books; the books went flying, he snarled and moved off. In the evening he turned up in my consulting room to apologise — British Birds, Catullus, The Holy War — and offered to fill the gap on my shelf. I turned to the shelf, and when I turned back, Sherlock Holmes was smiling at me across the table. I fainted — the first and last time in my life. “I owe you a thousand apologies, my dear Watson.”
demo.trace.return.desc:
Reread the entry of 4 May 1891. For three years I took it for the truth, and this is what really happened. Moriarty came alone; they grappled on the brink, Holmes slipped through his grip with a baritsu throw, and Moriarty fell. Holmes did not go back along the path — he climbed up the rock face so that everyone would think him dead: Moriarty still had men. From above, stones came flying at him — thrown by a confederate standing on the ledge. Holmes climbed down, walked ten miles through the night into Italy, and has lived under other names ever since. It was Park Lane that brought him back.
→ next: “The empty house”
demo.trace.moran.who.desc: Colonel Sebastian Moran, formerly of the Indian Army, the best heavy-game shot in the East, author of “Heavy Game of the Western Himalayas”; retired under a cloud, and Moriarty made him his chief of staff. It was he who threw the stones at Reichenbach. It was he who played cards with Adair — Adair caught him cheating and demanded that he leave the clubs — and it was he who shot Adair with the air-gun that the blind mechanic von Herder built for Moriarty. It fires a revolver bullet without a sound.
demo.trace.bust: A wax bust of Holmes in the window of 221B
demo.trace.bust.desc: Holmes ordered from Oscar Meunier of Grenoble a wax bust of himself and set it in the sitting-room window at Baker Street, with a lamp behind it. From the street below it is he — reading in his chair. Mrs. Hudson, on her knees so as to throw no shadow, turns the bust every quarter of an hour. She has been told there will be shooting.
demo.trace.moran.desc: We went into Camden House — the empty house opposite 221B — and waited in a dark room by the window. At midnight a man appeared in the street, came into the same house and took his stand at the next window: he had chosen this house too. He assembled the rifle, aimed at the bust and fired — a soft click and the tinkle of glass. Holmes sprang on him; I struck him with the butt of my revolver. Lestrade with two constables was waiting outside the door: “Glad to see you back in London, sir.” Holmes handed Colonel Moran over to them for the murder of Ronald Adair.
demo.trace.back.desc: In the spring I sold the Kensington practice to a young doctor named Verner — he paid an unexpectedly handsome price; some years later I learned that the money was Holmes's, and Verner a distant relation of his. I am back at Baker Street.
demo.trace.empty.case: One evening. No fee: Holmes was taking London back.
